## Policy

Policy rules are deny-only content constraints. They do not ask, and they cannot allow. A rule with no constraint denies whatever it matches. A rule with a constraint denies only when that constraint is violated. A deny is final (`POLICY_DENIED`, or `RECIPIENTS_UNKNOWN` and `ACCOUNT_DOMAIN_UNKNOWN` below).

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `planTtlSeconds` | `300` | A plan's lifetime: how long after `gws_plan` its commit tool accepts it. |
| `rules` | `[]` | Deny rules. Each needs `id` and `"effect": "deny"`. |

A rule may match `categories`, `accounts`, `services`, and `operations` (wildcards). It may set `allowedRecipientDomains`, `allowedRecipients`, `deniedRecipientDomains`, `allowExternalRecipients`, `allowPublicSharing`, `allowedReadRoots`, `allowedWriteRoots`, `maxPages`, and `maxItems`.

```jsonc
{
  "policy": {
    "rules": [
      {
        "id": "work-recipients",
        "effect": "deny",
        "categories": ["send", "share"],
        "accounts": ["work"],
        "allowedRecipientDomains": ["example.com"]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Recipients

The recipient constraints (`allowedRecipientDomains`, `allowedRecipients`, `deniedRecipientDomains`, `allowExternalRecipients: false`) check everyone a send or share reaches:

- Every address in `to`, `cc` and `bcc`, whether a list, a comma- or semicolon-separated string, `Name <address>`, or a group.
- The `To`, `Cc` and `Bcc` headers of a raw message (`gmail.users.messages.send`).
- What the request does not carry, read before the plan: the sender (or `Reply-To`) of the message a reply answers, and for reply-all its other recipients; a draft's stored recipients (`gmail.users.drafts.send`); an event's guests for a notifying change; a Drive permission's grantee. Each read needs `gws.read` on that method, and the commit reads them again: a plan whose recipients changed expires.
- A domain share (a Drive or Calendar ACL for a whole domain) counts as `*@<domain>`.

The check fails closed. When a matching rule limits recipients and the plugin cannot tell who the call reaches, the plan is refused with `RECIPIENTS_UNKNOWN`: a raw message without readable headers, a read that failed, an address it cannot read (such as a quoted local part), or a method whose recipients it does not know (Chat messages, Drive approvals). Scope such rules with `services` or `operations` when that is too broad. A share that only removes access reaches no one new.

"External" means outside the account's own domains: `accounts.<alias>.domains`, or else the domain of the signed-in address, which the plugin reads with Gmail, Drive or Calendar. A subdomain is a different domain. When neither is available the plan is refused with `ACCOUNT_DOMAIN_UNKNOWN`.

Deploy and watch are never committable, whatever a rule says. Admin is the admin gate, not a policy allow. See [admin.md](admin.md).

A Calendar event write (`insert`, `patch`, `update`, `move`, `quickAdd`) becomes `send` when it emails guests: `params.sendUpdates` is anything but `none`, or the deprecated `params.sendNotifications` is anything but `false`. A notifying `calendar.events.delete` stays `delete`, which asks every time and never offers Always. Calendar ACL changes, which notify by default, are already `share`. Drive `files.update` with `body.trashed` true becomes `delete`, including when the same body also renames the file. `gmail.send`, `gmail.reply`, `gmail.reply-all` and `gmail.forward` with `draft: true` become `write`: a draft reaches no one, so the plan lists no recipients and the recipient rules apply when `gmail.users.drafts.send` sends it. Commit with the plan's category, not the manifest category.

## Approvals

**Every tool is allowed by default.** The plugin inserts its default rules through `ctx.agent.transform`, immediately after each agent's base `{ "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" }` rule. An agent without that rule gets none, so its default deny stays a deny. The block is the `gws.*` namespace, then the five reads, then the six commits; the `access` option decides the effect, and the README prints the block for each value:

| `access` | The namespace and the six commits | The six read tools, events_list included, and the source reads probe, calendar_today and images_read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"all"` (the default) | `allow` | `allow` |
| `"ask-changes"` | `ask` | `allow` |
| `"read-only"` | `deny` | `allow` |

The namespace rule means a tool a later release adds follows the same value: allowed at `all`, asking at `ask-changes`, denied at `read-only`. A later rule wins, so a user's `permissions` rules and a saved Always override the block, and a stricter agent is not weakened.

Write and export offer Always for that exact `<account>:<operation>`. Send, share, delete, and admin pass no save patterns, so they never offer Always; at `ask-changes` they ask every time unless a user rule allows them.

With `rpcCommits` on, the same rules decide a script's commits through the tools RPC, except that a script's `ask` is refused, because no one can answer it. Off (the default), a script cannot commit at all.

`opencode run` cannot answer an ask. At `ask-changes`, give a commit a user allow rule there, for example `{ "action": "gws.write", "resource": "work:*", "effect": "allow" }`, or choose `all`. A user `deny` hides that tool. A Plan-style or custom deny such as `{ "action": "gws.*", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" }` still wins, because it is later than the inserted block.

An agent defined only in the user's config is created after plugins run, so it misses the inserted rules. That matters only when `access` holds something back. `/gws-status` and the status dialog then name those agents and show the block for the current value. Put it first in each listed agent's own `permissions`, in `opencode.json` or the agent's Markdown file, followed by your top-level rules for Google Workspace tools. Do not put the block in the top-level `permissions`: those rules apply after every agent's base rules and would loosen Explore.

`gws_status` gives the model only the count, `unguardedAgentCount`, and points to `/gws-status`.

Saved Always is stored by OpenCode for that exact resource. It applies across agents in the project, Plan included. A directory with no git commit belongs to the shared `global` project, so an Always saved there is not limited to one folder.

Plugin `policy` rules can only deny. They constrain recipients, public sharing, read and write roots, and page and item caps. They do not ask. Deploy and watch are never committable. Admin still needs `admin.enabled`, an allowed service, and a reason when `admin.requireReason` is set; the host ask is the human prompt.

Every permission rule in this document includes `resource`. A rule without it is skipped.

### Downloads outside the project

A download is written by the plugin, not by OpenCode's file tools, so the plugin asserts OpenCode's own `external_directory` permission for a destination outside the project, as well as `gws.export`. The resource is the destination's folder, and it is offered to Always:

```json
{ "action": "external_directory", "resource": "<folder>/*", "effect": "allow" }
```

A destination inside the project directory asserts nothing extra. An agent whose base rule allows everything allows `external_directory` too, so nothing asks there; a rule that asks or denies it makes the download ask, or refuse with `DOWNLOAD_NOT_PERMITTED`, whose next step is the rule above. The plugin's own `execution.allowedWriteRoots` still applies: it is checked before the host permission, and a path outside every root is `POLICY_DENIED`.

# In Jelly

[Jelly](https://heyjelly.ai) runs OpenCode agents. It reads the `jelly` section of this
package's `package.json` as JSON, without loading the plugin, when a person reviews the exact
version, and uses it as follows.

Jelly names the plugin **Google Workspace** (`jelly.title`), with the package name and version beneath. Under
that name it shows the one line in `jelly.summary`, and beside it the mark in `jelly.icon`
(`assets/icon.svg`, shipped in the package): Jelly reads that file once, when it records the
plugin, and keeps it only if it is a clean SVG of drawing elements, with no script, style, link
or outside reference. A Jelly whose declaration schema lacks `summary` or `icon` refuses this
declaration, because that schema accepts no unknown keys.

## Tools and permissions

12 tools are declared (6 read-only). Jelly's agents have no base "allow everything"
rule, so this plugin's own default rules, which it puts after that rule, never reach them. Jelly
writes each declared `ask` or `deny` as that tool's default instead (the person's own choice
replaces it), and denies a read-only helper every tool not marked `readOnly`. A declared `allow`
changes nothing in Jelly.

- Ask: none: every declared tool is allowed, as the plugin's default `access` is.
- Everything else runs. `gws.events_list` is for Memory's collector, which runs it unattended, so it never asks; it also asserts `gws.read` on each Gmail read it makes.

A commit still needs its plan: `gws_plan` returns a `planId`, and only the matching commit tool
applies it. The admin gate is on by default, and each admin plan needs an allowed service and a
reason. To make the commits ask, or stop them, the person sets the plugin's `access` option, or a
tool rule of their own in Jelly.

`test/jelly.test.ts` checks each declared effect against `defaultRules("all")`.

## Today's calendar

`jelly.nativeData` is `[{ "v": 1, "capability": "calendar", "view": "calendar-native", "read": "calendar.today", "source": "gws.calendar.today" }]`:
Jelly's own calendar reads the same method the **Today** tile calls, and draws it natively. `calendar.today` is
declared in `jelly.rpc` with `readOnly: true`, the label "read today's calendar", and the permission `gws.read`, the
permission `gws_read` already declares. Jelly calls it on the plugin's RPC named after the package,
`@joe-broadhead/opencode-gws`, through its core plugin's relay, with the input `{}`, and judges `gws.read` against
the agent's rules before the call reaches the plugin: an RPC call carries no session, so the plugin cannot ask
OpenCode itself. Outside Jelly, any client of the OpenCode server can call the method, as it can the status RPC.
The read therefore exposes event titles, locations and meeting links to any client of the OpenCode server, as the tools RPC can already reach `gws_read`, so serving OpenCode beyond localhost needs the server's own authentication.

`calendar.today` is deprecated until 0.1.0: the same read is the source contract's snapshot `gws.calendar.today`, the
method `calendar_today` on the tools RPC `google-workspace.gws.tools` (action `gws.calendar_today`), answering
`{ data: <agenda>, asOf, account, trust }` ([Sources](configuration.md#sources)). The hint names it:
`nativeData[0].source` is `gws.calendar.today`, so a Jelly with the source setting on reads Home's calendar from
`calendar_today`, and `view` and `read` stay for a Jelly without it (they go at contract version 2). The old method
answers as before for any other caller, and status says once it was called.

What it answers: `{ account, at, state, events }`.

- `account` is the alias of the account that answers: the implicit `default` account, or else the first configured
  account that enables `calendar`, interactive accounts before headless ones. It reads that account's primary
  calendar only and never says it checked another.
- Today is midnight to midnight in the primary calendar's own time zone, which the method reads from Google
  (`calendar.calendars.get`), not the machine's. A day with a clock change is 23 or 25 hours long.
- `events` are the entries of today not yet ended, at most 50, the earliest kept: `id` (Google's, or `sha256:<hex>`
  of one longer than 128 characters), `title` (at most 200 characters; "(No title)" when Google has none), `start`
  and `end` in UTC, `allDay: true` for an all-day entry (from the calendar's midnight to the next), and, when Google
  gives them, `location` (at most 200 characters), `url` (the event's Google Calendar link) and `joinUrl` (the
  event's Meet link, or else the video entry point of its conference). A link is kept only when it is https and
  carries no user name or password. Cancelled entries, entries the person declined and working-location entries are
  left out. Descriptions, guests and every other field are never read into the answer. The whole answer stays
  within 60 KB of JSON, under Jelly's 64 KB limit: when it would not, the latest-starting events are left out,
  whole, until it does, and the audit records how many as `omitted` on a `calendar.today` record.
- `state` is `ready` for a fresh reading. The method keeps its last good reading in memory and answers from it for a
  minute, so a tile that polls does not reach Google each time. When a later read fails, or takes more than eight
  seconds, it answers `stale` with the kept events of the same day and `at`, the time they were read. Nothing is
  written to disk.
- With nothing of today kept, a failure is the declared error `failed`, with the plugin's code and next step:
  `AUTH_REQUIRED` or `AUTH_SCOPE_MISSING` when the account must sign in (these also drop the kept reading, so a
  signed-out calendar is never shown as stale), `CALENDAR_UNAVAILABLE` when no account enables `calendar`, and
  the read's own code otherwise. Jelly shows any failure as "not available".

The method runs two reads through the plugin's read path, with the account's own sign-in and the read policy, as
`gws_read` does: `calendar.calendars.get` (`fields: timeZone`) and one page of `calendar.events.list` (single
events in start order, at most 250, with a field mask). It never downloads gws: when no verified copy is cached yet, the
method fails with `GWS_UNAVAILABLE`. A day with more than 250 entries is cut at 250.

`test/calendar.test.ts` checks the declaration against Jelly's native data rules, and the method against fake
Calendar answers; `test/host/calendar.test.ts` calls it on a real OpenCode host.

## Pictures in an agent's UI

`jelly.imageHosts` lists exactly the hosts the method takes: `drive.google.com` and Google's own image servers,
`lh3` to `lh7`, `lh7-rt` and `lh7-us` under `googleusercontent.com`, each by its full name. `jelly.imageRead` is
`{ "method": "images.read" }`: when an agent's UI shows a picture whose address is on one of those hosts, Jelly asks
this plugin for it, and the window never gets the address or a token. `images.read` is declared in `jelly.rpc` with
`readOnly: true`, the label "read a Google Workspace picture", and the permission `gws.read`, the one `gws_read`
declares. Jelly calls it on the RPC named after the package with `{ url }`, the picture's address, after judging
`gws.read` against the agent's rules: an ask or a deny shows no picture, and nobody is asked. Outside Jelly, any
client of the OpenCode server can call the method, as it can `calendar.today`.

What it answers: `{ mime, base64 }`, a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP of at most 1 MB. The type comes from the picture's first
bytes, never from a `Content-Type` or Drive's `mimeType`; SVG, HTML and every other kind are `IMAGE_TYPE_REFUSED`. A
picture over 1 MB is `IMAGE_TOO_LARGE`: the plugin stops reading at that size and answers nothing, never a picture cut
short. Jelly checks the answer again before it draws it.

Which addresses it takes. The address must be https, with no user name, password, port or IP address, on
`drive.google.com` or one of those image servers; anything else is `IMAGE_HOST_REFUSED`, and nothing is fetched. Any
other `googleusercontent.com` name is refused too: Apps Script pages and every Compute Engine machine's reverse DNS
name live there, so a prompt-injected agent could otherwise put data in a picture address and have the person's
machine send it to a server anyone can run. The plugin checks this itself, whatever Jelly checked.

- **A Drive link** (`https://drive.google.com/file/d/<id>/…`, `/open?id=`, `/uc?id=` or `/thumbnail?id=`) is never
  fetched. The plugin reads the file through gws, as the account, with the read policy and the audit, as `gws_read`
  does: `drive.files.get` with `fields: mimeType,size,thumbnailLink`, then, for a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP of at most
  1 MB, its bytes (`alt=media`). gws writes those bytes to a file in a private directory under the plugin's work
  folder, which the plugin reads back with the cap and removes before it answers. Any other file, and a picture over
  1 MB, answers its thumbnail; a file with neither is `IMAGE_UNAVAILABLE`.
- **An image-server address** (a Drive `thumbnailLink`, a Docs or Slides picture, a profile photo) is fetched over HTTPS by
  the plugin itself: gws reads Google's APIs, not an arbitrary address. A redirect is never followed, any answer but
  200 is `IMAGE_UNAVAILABLE`, no cookie or referrer is sent, and the size is checked while the body streams.

Where the account's token goes. Only to those image servers, and only for an address Google returned to that account
in this process: the plugin remembers, in memory for an hour, the addresses in the fields Google itself fills with a
picture or file link (Drive's `thumbnailLink`, `iconLink`, `webViewLink`, `webContentLink` and a user's `photoLink`,
Docs' `contentUri`, Slides' `contentUrl`, People's `photos[].url` and `coverPhotos[].url`, the Directory's
`thumbnailPhotoUrl`), at most 1,000, never the bytes. Text that people write, such as a document, a cell, an event's
description or a slide's `sourceUrl`, never counts. An image-server address Google did not return is fetched without
credentials, so a private picture there shows nothing. A credentials-file account's token stays inside gws, so its
pictures come only from Drive links.

Which account reads it: the one Google returned the address to; else the only account that enables `drive`; else the
`default` account when it is one of them. Otherwise it is `IMAGE_ACCOUNT_AMBIGUOUS`, and the plugin never tries each
account in turn. An account must also enable `drive` for its token to be used. When that account is signed out, the
answer is `AUTH_REQUIRED`; Jelly shows no picture, and its card for this plugin asks the person to sign in.

At most four pictures are read at once (one more is `IMAGE_UNAVAILABLE`), and each gives up after eight seconds,
inside Jelly's ten. A failure is the declared error `failed`, with the plugin's code and next step; Jelly shows any
failure as no picture. No error, log line or audit record names the address, the file or the token: an
`images.read` audit record notes only the outcome, the account, the duration and the code.

Jelly's limit today: Jelly's picture contract allows 1 MB (`AGENT_UI_IMAGE_MAX_BYTES`), but its host refuses any plugin
RPC answer over 64 KB of JSON (`VIEW_DATA_MAX_BYTES`), so a picture over about 47 KB, which base64 makes larger than
that, shows no picture in Jelly until Jelly lifts that limit for pictures. The plugin answers the whole picture
regardless; the limit is Jelly's.

`test/images.test.ts` checks the address gate, the token hosts, the cap while streaming, the type from the bytes, the
account rule and the declaration against Jelly's rules, all against fake answers with no network.

## Changes a person approves in an agent's UI

Off by default. `jelly.actions` declares one action, `commit`, with `ui: true`, so an agent can bind it to a button in
a UI it makes. It is plan-shaped: its input is a gws plan request, the same shape `gws_plan` takes, and this release
allows only one operation, a Sheets value update:

```json
{
  "account": "work",
  "operation": "sheets.spreadsheets.values.update",
  "params": { "spreadsheetId": "<id>", "range": "Invoices!D2:D3", "valueInputOption": "RAW" },
  "body": { "values": [["Paid"], ["Paid"]] }
}
```

To turn it on, list the operation in the plugin's options: `"uiActions": ["sheets.spreadsheets.values.update"]`. The
list takes no other value yet; a later release that supports more operations never turns them on for someone who
listed this one.

What the declaration says. Label "update cells in your Google Sheets"; `class: "local"`, so only an owner device can
take it; `confirm: "always"`, so Jelly asks every time; `summary: ["account", "params"]`; `preview: "plan.preview"`;
`tool: "gws.write"`, because an agent makes the same change with `gws_plan` then `gws_write`. It declares no `done`,
because Jelly's `{count}` is how many rows the person picked, not how many cells changed; the receipt says the label.

**The preview.** `plan.preview` is declared in `jelly.rpc` with `readOnly: true` and the permission `gws.plan`, so a
rule that denies `gws.plan` also stops the preview. Given the same input, it runs gws's own plan path (the account,
the service, every policy rule, the admin gate and the recipient rules) and `gws --dry-run`, stores no plan, and
answers in words: the category and operation, the account, the method and address, the spreadsheet and range, and
every cell it writes, row by row. Each field the agent wrote stays on its own line in reading order: the spreadsheet,
the range and every cell are quoted, and a control character, a line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029) or a
bidi mark, embedding, override or isolate is shown as a visible `\uXXXX` escape, so a field cannot fake or reorder
a line. Those values are the input's own; they are shown to the person, never logged or audited. When the words would
be over the 4,000 characters Jelly's confirmation shows, the preview refuses rather than cut them short, and Jelly
then offers only Not now.

The preview is a dry run: it needs no grant, changes nothing, and writes no audit record. Like `calendar.today` and
`images.read`, any client of the OpenCode server can call it; it still refuses when `uiActions` does not list the
operation or `access` is `read-only`.

**The action.** Jelly's core plugin calls `act.commit` on the RPC named after the package with `{ input, grant }`. In
order, the plugin:

1. checks Jelly's grant, as Jelly's own verifier does: Jelly's action key (published in the engine), this plugin,
   the action `commit`, the digest of exactly this input, at most 60 seconds old, and never used before; the
   class must be `local`, and the grant's `cfm`, the confirmation Jelly drew before the person chose, must be
   `always`: a grant without one, or with `never` or `session`, is `UI_GRANT_REFUSED` before anything reaches Google.
   In stock OpenCode there is no Jelly key, so nothing can take the action;
2. refuses any operation but `sheets.spreadsheets.values.update`, `USER_ENTERED` (a value would be read as a
   formula, and a formula can send the sheet's contents elsewhere), any extra field, and more than 100 rows of 26
   cells (`UI_ACTION_REFUSED`);
3. refuses when `uiActions` does not list the operation (`UI_ACTION_OFF`), or `access` is `read-only`
   (`UI_ACTION_REFUSED`); at `ask-changes` it runs, because the person's every-time confirmation is the ask;
4. plans the change as the person, in a plan bound to this grant alone, through the same path as `gws_plan`, and
   commits it, single-use, as `gws_write` does;
5. answers what Google says changed: `{ account, operation, spreadsheetId, updatedRange, updatedRows,
   updatedColumns, updatedCells }`.

Every call, refused ones included, writes a `ui.act` audit record with `caller: "person"`, the Jelly member whose
device approved it (`member`, the grant's `mbr`) and the grant's id (`grant`, its `jti`); the plan and commit
records carry the same three. No record holds the values, the spreadsheet or the range.

**Whose rules apply.** On this path the person is acting, not an agent. The plugin's own settings apply: `access`
(read-only refuses), `uiActions`, the policy rules and the admin gate. The person's OpenCode permission rules for
agents are not consulted, because no agent or session makes the call: a rule of their own that denies or asks for
`gws_write` (or `gws.write`) holds an agent's commits, not this one. To stop it, leave `uiActions` empty, set
`access` to `read-only`, or add a policy rule that denies the change.

What the plugin cannot check yet, and has asked Jelly for:

- **That the preview was shown.** The grant binds the input, and the preview is worked out from that same input, so
  what is committed is what the preview describes; but nothing in the grant says the preview was drawn.
- **The receipt.** Jelly words it from the rows picked; the plugin's answer says what changed.
- **Whose Google account.** The grant names a Jelly member, not a Google account; owner devices only is the guard.

Jelly also gives an act ten seconds in all. The action runs a dry run and then the commit; when Google is slow, Jelly
can give up after the change was made. Check the sheet before asking again.

`test/ui-action.test.ts` checks every refusal above, that the preview is the plan the commit runs, the audit records,
and the declaration against Jelly's action rules.

## Signing in

`jelly.signIns` declares one sign-in, `google`, for OpenCode's integration `gws-*`: every account (`gws-<alias>`) folds into it, so the card waits while any account waits. The sign-in declares what Jelly does for it, so Jelly has no code of its own for gws:

- `account`: Jelly asks for an account's name and writes `{ "mode": "interactive" }` under it in `accounts`; gws has no account until one is named, so Jelly adds it to an agent with that question and never gives it blank. That account names no `enabledServices`, so it gets every service the `default` account enables, and its form starts on Read-only and still offers Read and write.
- `hostClient`: `{ "id": "google", "field": "clientJson", "replaces": ["clientId", "clientSecret"] }`. Jelly holds the person's OAuth clients and answers the hidden `clientJson` field with one, whole: the Desktop app client for a loopback sign-in. Its form shows only Access (starting on `default`, read-only) and the write acknowledgement while it applies, and no `oauthClient` option is needed.
- `needed`: `AUTH_REQUIRED` and `AUTH_SCOPE_MISSING`, the codes a gws tool result carries when an account must sign in again, so Jelly puts this card in front of the person.

These need Jelly 0.3.2 or later; an older Jelly refuses the declaration's new keys. When the engine runs on another machine than the person's browser, a host can also fill the form's hidden `redirectUri` and `callbackPort` fields, and answer `clientJson` with a Web application client that lists the redirect, so Google's redirect comes back through the host to the engine's listener; see [docs/auth.md](auth.md#sign-in-when-opencode-runs-on-another-machine). The sign-in declares `"relay": { "redirectField": "redirectUri", "portField": "callbackPort" }`: those are the two fields a Jelly web tab fills with its fixed relay address at Jelly ID and a loopback port for the listener (Jelly ADR 0019). The plugin's code is the same either way, and the Web application client must list that relay address.

Jelly folds the declared sign-ins into this plugin's one card, which shows each as Connected, Not signed in or Sign in again (expired or revoked), and starts, renews and signs out of each. An agent's `jelly_connection_request`, or a tool result that names this plugin's "Run /connect and choose …" next step, opens the same card. The plugin still signs in through OpenCode, as it does without Jelly; the declaration only tells Jelly which of the engine's integrations and servers are this plugin's.

The account's name on the card is its verified email: the method's `label` is the email Google returned at sign-in, else the alias. OpenCode keeps the label it gets at sign-in, so an account signed in with an earlier release shows its alias until the person signs it in again.

**An agent's copy.** The person signs in once, in their own engine; an agent given the account gets Jelly's copy of that sign-in (D210): the access token, `jelly-host-owns-refresh` in place of the refresh token, an expiry a day ahead, and every metadata key but the secret-named ones, so the client secret stays with the person. Every call reads the copy as it reads a sign-in: the token, the access level, the scopes Google granted, the email and the domain, which is all a tool, status, `/gws-status` or the source contract's `probe` needs. The client is read only to renew or to sign in again. Jelly renews the person's sign-in in their engine and puts the next copy in before this one runs out; the plugin reads the credential from OpenCode on every call and keeps no token, so it uses the new copy at once. If OpenCode ever asks the plugin to renew a copy (the refresh token is `jelly-host-owns-refresh`), it refuses with `AUTH_REQUIRED` and the sign-in-again step, without calling Google, and Jelly puts this card in front of the person. A sign-in without its client secret is never renewed either.

**Headless accounts are outside Jelly.** Jelly adds only interactive accounts. A `credentials_file` account hands gws a credentials file, and gws exchanges it for a token and caches that token, encrypted, in the plugin's own per-account directory, by design; an `access_token` account reads its environment variable, whose value is fixed when OpenCode starts. Neither is read from OpenCode's credential store, so neither is a copy Jelly can put in or replace.

# Scripting

Unofficial plugin. Not affiliated with Google.

A script can call the gws tools with no model: a cron job, a shell script, or any program that can reach the OpenCode
server. It uses the tools RPC, `google-workspace.gws.tools`, through `opencode api` or an OpenCode client.

Each read tool is a method, with the same name, input and output. A `gws_read` call and the `read` method with the same
input are the same call: the same policy, errors and permission checks. The six commit tools are not methods, unless
the host turns on [`rpcCommits`](configuration.md#plugin-options) because it confirms changes itself. Without it, a script
can plan a change, but only the model's approved commit tool runs the plan, so a script never commits on its own.

| Method | The tool |
| --- | --- |
| `status` | `gws_status` |
| `catalog` | `gws_catalog` |
| `schema` | `gws_schema` |
| `read` | `gws_read` |
| `plan` | `gws_plan` |
| `events_list` | Code Mode only: the Gmail messages or Calendar events since a cursor, as the source contract's events ([configuration.md](configuration.md#events-list)) |
| `probe`, `calendar_today`, `images_read` | none: the source contract's probe and its two snapshot reads, `gws.calendar.today` and `gws.image`, each with its own read action ([Sources](configuration.md#sources)) |
| `write`, `send`, `share`, `delete`, `export`, `admin` | Only with `rpcCommits`: `gws_write`, `gws_send`, `gws_share`, `gws_delete`, `gws_export` and `gws_admin`, each taking only `{ planId }` ([Plans and commits](#plans-and-commits)) |
| `describe` | none: lists the methods with their class and their input and output as JSON Schema; with `sessionID`, each method also reports its resolved `permission` |

## A script runs as a session

Every call names a session, and the session must name an agent. The script runs as that agent: each call asserts the
same action and resource as the tool, against the agent's permission rules and the session's own.

**A rule decides, before anything runs.** The RPC resolves the method's action against the agent's rules and then the
session's, with the host's order (the last matching rule wins). Only an `allow` runs. An `ask` is refused, because no
one is there to answer the prompt, and a `deny` is refused. A refusal costs nothing: no gws call, no credential, no
prompt left waiting.

A script gets the same default as the model: every method is allowed, because the agent's block allows the reads. A rule
on the agent or the session can still deny a method, and a denied method is refused before anything runs. Without
`rpcCommits` a script never commits a plan, so the plugin's `access` option restricts the model's commits, not the
script's calls. With it, `access` decides the script's commits too: allowed at `"all"`; at `"ask-changes"` (the ask
has no one to answer it) and at `"read-only"` refused unless a rule explicitly allows the action. The last matching
rule wins, and the session's rules come after the agent's, which come after the plugin's block, so an allow on the
agent or the session overrides the block's ask or deny, and a deny there overrides an allow.

A saved **Always allow** does not authorise an ad-hoc script. It is not part of the agent's or the session's rules, so
the resolve never sees it. That is deliberate: a script's permission must be reviewable in config. The supported way to
get an approval-bound grant is a Jobs one-off script (`jobs_run_script`), whose approval names the exact methods.

Create the session once, with the agent the script should run as, and keep its id. Give the project as the session's `location`: a session made without one belongs to the service's default location, where the project's agents may not exist, and each call then fails `Agent not found`:

```sh
opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"mail digest","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"}}'
```

Session rules come after the agent's, so a session can narrow what its script may do, or opt one method in:

```sh
opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"label sorter","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"},"permissions":[
  {"action":"gws.*","resource":"*","effect":"deny"},
  {"action":"gws.read","resource":"*","effect":"allow"},
  {"action":"gws.plan","resource":"*","effect":"allow"}
]}'
```

The reads and `plan` are always allowed by the plugin's block, whatever `access` is. The six commit actions follow
`access`: allowed by default, asking at `ask-changes`, denied at `read-only`. That decides the model's commits and,
with [`rpcCommits`](#committing-from-a-script-rpccommits), a script's. The session above
denies the namespace and opts the reads and `plan` back in, so the script can look and plan, and nothing else.

Ask `describe` for the methods, with their classes and schemas, and with the session each method's permission:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/google-workspace.gws.tools/describe \
  -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…"}}'
```

`describe` takes nothing, or `{"sessionID": "…"}`. Each call is resolved against its session's agent when it runs, so a refusal names the rule.

## The location

Run the command in the project whose agent you mean, and send the call to that location explicitly:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/google-workspace.gws.tools/read \
  -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…","input":{"operation":"users.get","params":{"userId":"me"}}}}'
```

Without it the call goes to the service's default location and fails `rpc.unavailable` if the plugin is not loaded
there. The HTTP equivalents are the `location[directory]` query parameter and the same header. `describe` reports the
`location` that answered and a `locationHint`.

A location unloads after OpenCode's idle timeout. If a scheduled script gets `rpc.unavailable` from a location that was
loaded before, send the call again once: the request loads the location. Jobs keeps its own location loaded.

## Calling a method

The body is `{"input": {"sessionID": "<session>", "input": <the tool's input>}}`:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/google-workspace.gws.tools/read \
  -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{
  "sessionID":"ses_…",
  "input":{"operation":"gmail.users.messages.list","params":{"userId":"me","q":"after:1767225600 before:1767312000"},"fields":"messages(id),nextPageToken"}
}}'
```

A result is the tool's own output, as plain JSON. A read's `data` is the parsed JSON response, or a string when the call
returns text: a helper run with `format` `table`, `yaml` or `csv`, `gmail.triage` (a table unless `format` is `json`),
or `gmail.read` (text unless `format` is `json`). Workspace content in it is untrusted data.

## Plans and commits

`plan` returns a plan bound to the account, the session and its agent, as `gws_plan` does. By default a script cannot
commit it: the six commit tools are not methods, and calling one answers `rpc.method_not_found`. The model commits the
plan with its approved commit tool (`gws_write`, `gws_send`, `gws_share`, `gws_delete`, `gws_export` or `gws_admin`),
which asserts that commit's action, and at `access: "ask-changes"` OpenCode asks the person first. An export whose
destination is outside the project also asserts OpenCode's own `external_directory`, so a session that asks for that
folder refuses the export (`DOWNLOAD_NOT_PERMITTED`) before gws runs. A plan is single-use and bound to its session:
another session cannot commit it (`PLAN_CALLER_MISMATCH`).

### Committing from a script: `rpcCommits`

A host that shows its own confirmation for each change, before it calls the RPC, can set the plugin option
`"rpcCommits": true`. The six commit tools are then methods too, named by category, with the classes `describe` reports:
`write` (write), `send` and `share` (send), `delete` and `admin` (destructive), and `export` (export). Each takes only
`{ planId }` and runs the commit tool's own spec, so nothing about a plan changes:

- the plan must come from `plan` in the same session, with the same agent and account (`PLAN_CALLER_MISMATCH`);
- it commits once (`PLAN_ALREADY_USED`), and only through its own category's method (`CATEGORY_MISMATCH`, which leaves
  the plan ready for the right one);
- the method's action (`gws.send`, …) is resolved like any other, so at `access: "ask-changes"` a commit is refused with
  `PERMISSION_DENIED` and no gws call, and at `"read-only"` it is denied, unless a later rule on the agent or the
  session allows the action;
- a reply, a draft or an event's guests are read again at the commit, as on the model path.

The plugin asks no one before such a commit: the host's confirmation is the only one. Leave the option off unless the
host gives one. Status says whether it is on: `rpcCommits` in `gws_status` and the status RPC, and the **Script
commits** row in `/gws-status` and the status dialog.

With the option on, a script commits a plan only when the commit's action resolves to `allow` for its session. At the
default `access: "all"` the plugin's block allows it. At `"ask-changes"` the block asks, so the commit is refused unless
a rule allows it explicitly. A session can opt one category in; the rule must cover every resource (`"resource": "*"`),
because the RPC resolves the method's action before it knows the plan's account and operation:

```sh
opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"replies","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"},"permissions":[
  {"action":"gws.send","resource":"*","effect":"allow"}
]}'
```

The same holds at `"read-only"`: the block denies every commit, but the last matching rule wins, so an explicit allow
on the agent or the session still lets a script commit. A rule that denies the action, on the agent or the session,
refuses the commit at any `access`, unless a later rule (the session's comes last) allows it again.

**`rpcCommits` trusts every caller of the OpenCode server.** The permission check guards which session a call runs
as, not who makes the call: any caller of the server API can create a session, choose its agent, and give it session
rules that allow every commit, then plan and commit in it. So `access` and the rules hold back the model and a
well-behaved script, not a caller of the server. Turn the option on only where every caller of the server is trusted:
a local server, or one behind authentication you control.

**A plan is bound to its session and agent, not to whether a script or the model made it.** A script that is given the
id of a model's session, and runs as that session's agent, can commit the plans pending in it, if the commit's action
resolves to `allow` there. Keep session ids to the callers that may act for that session.

**Agents without the default rules.** An agent defined only in the user's config misses the plugin's block (see
[Approvals](configuration.md#approvals)); with a generic allow, its commits are allowed with no ask, for a script too.
With `rpcCommits` on, status names those agents: `rpcCommitsUnguardedAgents` in `gws_status`, `unguardedAgents` in the
status RPC, the **Script commits** row in `/gws-status` and the status dialog, and a note in each commit method's
`describe` description.

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/google-workspace.gws.tools/plan \
  -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…","input":{"operation":"gmail.reply","input":{"messageId":"…","body":"Thanks."}}}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/google-workspace.gws.tools/send \
  -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…","input":{"planId":"<the planId plan returned>"}}}'
```

## Errors

A refusal or failure is the RPC error `failed`, with `data: { code, next }` from the
[error table](configuration.md#errors): the tool's own codes, plus a few for scripts.

| Code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `SESSION_UNKNOWN` | OpenCode says the session does not exist in this location. Any other failure to look the session up is OpenCode's own error, passed through unchanged. |
| `SESSION_AGENT_REQUIRED` | The session names no agent, or the agent does not exist. |
| `PERMISSION_DENIED` | The agent's or the session's rules ask or deny the call. The message says which, and names an inner action when one is refused, such as a plan's read of an event's guests. |
| `CANCELLED` | The call was aborted. |

A commit method, with `rpcCommits`, adds the plan's own codes: `PLAN_NOT_FOUND`, `PLAN_EXPIRED`, `PLAN_ALREADY_USED`,
`PLAN_CALLER_MISMATCH` and `CATEGORY_MISMATCH`.

OpenCode itself answers `rpc.method_not_found` for a method that does not exist (a commit method too, without
`rpcCommits`), and `rpc.invalid_input` for a bad
envelope, with one message per problem, in the wording every plugin's tools RPC uses:

| Case | Message |
| --- | --- |
| The envelope (the body's `input`) is not an object | `the envelope must be an object, such as {"sessionID":"<session>","input":<the tool's input>}` |
| An unknown key, such as `extra` | `"extra" is not allowed` |
| `sessionID` missing, not a string, or empty | `"sessionID" must be a non-empty string` |
| `input` missing | `"input" is missing` |
| `describe` given anything but nothing, `{}`, or `{"sessionID": "…"}` | `describe takes nothing, or {"sessionID":"<session>"}` |

The tool's own input is checked by the tool, as `GWS_VALIDATION_ERROR`; the source reads (`events_list`, `probe`,
`calendar_today`, `images_read`) refuse it as the source contract does, with `INPUT_INVALID`, and an unknown source with
`SOURCE_UNKNOWN`.

`opencode api` exits with status 1 on any RPC error, and prints the error body, so a shell script can test `$?` and
read `data.code`.

## Audit

A script's reads, plans and commits are audited like the tools', with `caller: "rpc"`.

Unofficial plugin. Not affiliated with Google.

The TUI is one status dialog. It cannot approve or commit a plan. Neither can the RPC or the commands.

## Status dialog

The palette command **Google Workspace: Status**, or `/gws` in the prompt, opens one dialog. Nothing is always visible: the plugin adds no footer, sidebar or other slot. The dialog and `/gws-status` show the same rows, in this order:

| Row | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Connection | per account: `connected`, `sign-in required`, or `not configured` (a headless account whose environment variable is unset) |
| Account | the alias and how it signs in: OpenCode sign-in, credentials file, or access token |
| Access | `read-only` or `read and write`, then the client, services, and granted and missing scopes |
| Hidden skills | only when another skill file uses one of the plugin's skill ids, which hides the plugin's own: the id and that file |
| Shell gws skills | only when another skill teaches agents to run `gws` in a shell, which skips plans, approvals and policy: each id and its file |
| Tools | the services whose gws tools the model sees |
| Permissions | the posture from `access`: every tool runs without asking, each commit asks, or the commits are denied |
| Script commits | from `rpcCommits`: `off`, a script can plan but not commit; or `on`, a script can commit a plan when its rules allow the commit, with no prompt from the plugin; when on, it also names the agents without the default rules, whose scripts commit without asking |
| Agents without default rules | their names, then the rules to put first in each agent's own `permissions` |
| OpenCode | the version, then `(tested)`, or `(host untested; supported range >=2.2.3 <2.4.0)` |
| Next step | exactly one; `Nothing to do.` when nothing is needed |

The key hint reads `r refresh · esc close`. The dialog listens for server reconnects and integration, credential and agent changes only while it is open. It loads nothing while closed, and it reads only the `status` RPC.

## Commands

Each command posts a message and does not start a model turn.

| Command | What it posts |
| --- | --- |
| `/gws-status` | The status model: each account's mode, access, client source, granted and missing scopes, and next step; the Google Cloud steps for accounts that have no OAuth client yet; this session's pending plans, redacted (category, operation, account, preview, expiry; never argv, a body, or a token); the permission posture, agents without the default rules, by name, then the rules to add first in each one's own permissions; and one next step. |

## RPC

Contract: `src/rpc.ts`, id `google-workspace.gws`, method `status` only. It is internal: the build inlines it into both `dist/index.js` and `dist/tui.js`, and the package exports only `.` and `./tui`.

`status` returns the fields every plugin's status RPC shares (`version`, `host`, `state`, `unguardedAgents`, `nextStep`), with the plugin's own beside them:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `version` | This package's version. |
| `host` | `{ version, range, tested }`: the OpenCode version (`null` when unknown), the supported range `>=2.2.3 <2.4.0`, and `true` only for a tested release (2.2.3, 2.2.4, 2.2.5, 2.2.6, 2.2.7, 2.3.0). |
| `state` | `sign_in_required` when an interactive account needs signing in, `not_configured` when a headless account's variable is unset, else `connected`. An untested OpenCode release inside the range keeps this state; only `host.tested` and the OpenCode row mark it. |
| `access` | What the default rules allow, from the plugin option: `all`, `ask-changes` or `read-only`. The dialog and `/gws-status` show it as **Permissions**. |
| `rpcCommits` | Whether the six commit tools are also tools RPC methods, from the plugin option. The dialog and `/gws-status` show it as **Script commits**, which, when it is on, also names the `unguardedAgents`. `gws_status` carries those names as `rpcCommitsUnguardedAgents` when it is on. |
| `gws` | `{ path, version }` of the resolved binary. |
| `services` | Model-facing services. |
| `accounts` | One entry per account, below. |
| `auditDegraded` | Present when the audit sink has failed. Omitted means false. |
| `shadowedSkills` | `[{ id, path }]`: skills OpenCode lists under one of the plugin's skill ids but from another file, so the plugin's own does not load. Present when any does. |
| `shellSkills` | `[{ id, path }]`: skills OpenCode lists, other than the plugin's own, whose text runs `gws` in a shell: a line in a fenced code block, or an inline code span, that starts with `gws ` and a word (`gws gmail +triage`). Prose that only names gws does not count. Present when any does. |
| `unguardedAgents` | Agents that missed the default rules while `access` holds something back, so a commit there runs without asking. Empty at `all`, where nothing is held back. |
| `permissionsBlock` | The JSON block to add first in each of those agents' own `permissions`. Present when `unguardedAgents` is not empty. |
| `nextStep` | The one thing to do next, as one sentence: an account's sign-in step, then a hidden skill, then the skills that run gws in a shell, then the unguarded agents. `Nothing to do.` when nothing is needed. |

An account entry is `{ alias, mode, services, integrationID?, connected, needsAuth?, access?, clientSource?, grantedScopes?, email?, domain?, missingScopes?, delegationRequired?, nextStep? }`. `email` and `domain` are the signed-in account's verified email and Workspace domain, from its sign-in's `id_token` once its `iss`, `aud` and `exp` check out ([auth.md](auth.md#after-sign-in)); the dialog and `/gws-status` do not show them. `delegationRequired` names the enabled services that need domain-wide delegation (Keep) when the interactive account's scopes do not add them; the dialog and `/gws-status` show it as **Needs domain-wide delegation**.

- `connected` is true when an interactive account is signed in and usable, or when a headless account's environment variable is set. `/gws-doctor` checks the headless credential itself.
- `needsAuth` is `true` or absent.
- `access` (on an account) is the signed-in level, or the form's default before sign-in.
- `clientSource` is `account`, `plugin`, or `pasted` (entered in the sign-in form).
- An account's `nextStep` is one sentence, absent when nothing is needed.

The status RPC cannot approve or commit. A commit happens when the agent calls a commit tool, which runs without a prompt at the default `access` and needs the permission prompt's allow at `ask-changes`, or, only with `rpcCommits`, when a script calls a commit method of the tools RPC ([scripting.md](scripting.md#committing-from-a-script-rpccommits)).

Scripts call the tools through a separate RPC, `google-workspace.gws.tools`: see [Scripting](scripting.md).

A third RPC, named after the package (`@joe-broadhead/opencode-gws`), has two read-only methods for Jelly: `calendar.today`, for Jelly's calendar ([In Jelly](jelly.md#todays-calendar)), and `images.read`, which draws a Google Drive or Workspace picture in an agent's UI ([In Jelly](jelly.md#pictures-in-an-agents-ui)).
